en: Thus have I heard: the Discourse on Right View (Sammādiṭṭhisutta), the ninth in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus!”
“Friends,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“‘Right view, right view,’ friends, it is said.”
"To what extent, friends, is a noble disciple one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and who has arrived at this true Dhamma?
"Friends, we would have traveled even from afar to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement.
It would be well indeed if the Venerable Sāriputta himself were to clarify the meaning of this statement."
“Having heard it from the Venerable Sāriputta, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, friends, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

"Friends, when a noble disciple understands the unwholesome and understands the root of the unwholesome, and understands the wholesome and understands the root of the wholesome—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma."
"But what, friends, is the unwholesome? What is the root of the unwholesome? What is the wholesome? What is the root of the wholesome?
Killing living beings, friends, is unwholesome; taking what is not given is unwholesome; sexual misconduct is unwholesome;
false speech is unwholesome; malicious speech is unwholesome; harsh speech is unwholesome; idle chatter is unwholesome."
Covetousness is unwholesome, ill will is unwholesome, wrong view is unwholesome— this, friends,
is called the unwholesome.
And what, friends, is the root of the unwholesome?
Greed is a root of unwholesomeness, hatred is a root of unwholesomeness, and delusion is a root of unwholesomeness—
this, friends, is called a root of unwholesomeness.
And what, friends, is wholesome?
Abstaining from taking life is wholesome; abstaining from taking what is not given is wholesome; abstaining from sexual misconduct is wholesome;
abstaining from false speech is wholesome; abstaining from malicious speech is wholesome;
abstaining from harsh speech is wholesome; abstaining from idle chatter is wholesome; non-covetousness is wholesome; non-ill will is wholesome.
Right view is wholesome—
this, friends, is called the wholesome.
And what, friends, is the root of the wholesome?
Non-greed is a root of the wholesome, non-hatred is a root of the wholesome, and non-delusion is a root of the wholesome—
this, friends, is called a root of the wholesome. When, friends,
a noble disciple understands unwholesomeness in this way and understands the root of unwholesomeness in this way, [he is said to be one who has understood.]
Thus he understands what is wholesome; thus he understands the root of the wholesome.

Having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust in every way, having removed the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the conceit and view of "I am," and having abandoned ignorance and generated true knowledge, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
"Excellent, friend," those bhikkhus said, rejoicing and expressing their appreciation for the Venerable Sāriputta’s words, and they asked the Venerable Sāriputta a further question:
“Could there be, friend, another way in which a noble disciple possesses right view, whose view is upright, who is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma?
“There could be, friend.
When, friend, a noble disciple understands nutriment, understands the origin of nutriment, understands the cessation of nutriment, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of nutriment—”
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friend, is nutriment? What is the origin of nutriment? What is the cessation of nutriment? What is the practice leading to the cessation of nutriment?
There are these four nutriments, friend, for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth."
Which four? Edible food, whether gross or subtle; second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness.

With the arising of craving comes the arising of nutriment; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of nutriment. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, namely: [the eight factors].
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness,
and right concentration. Friend, when a noble disciple thus understands nutriment, thus understands the origin of nutriment, thus understands the cessation of nutriment,
and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, he [is completely]...

Having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, having dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the view and conceit “I am,” having abandoned ignorance and generated true knowledge, one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” those bhikkhus said, rejoicing and expressing their appreciation for the Venerable Sāriputta’s words, and they asked him a further question:

“But, friend, could there be another way in which a noble disciple possesses right view, whose view is upright, who is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, and who has arrived at this true Dhamma?
“There could be, friend.”

"Friends, when a noble disciple understands suffering, understands the origin of suffering, understands the cessation of suffering, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friends, is suffering? What is the origin of suffering? What is the cessation of suffering? What is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?"
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering;
association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not to obtain what one desires is suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
This, friends, is called suffering.
And what, friends, is the origin of suffering?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is to say:—
Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence— this, friends,
is called the origin of suffering.
And what, friends, is the cessation of suffering?
The complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, its renunciation, its liberation, and its non-attachment— this, friends,
is called the cessation of suffering.
And what, friends, is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
This very Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration—this, friends, is called the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands suffering, thus understands the origin of suffering, thus understands the cessation of suffering,
and thus understands the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,
he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, dispels the underlying tendency to aversion, and uproots the underlying tendency to the conceit and view of "I am."
"By abandoning ignorance and arousing true knowledge, one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
"Excellent, friend," those bhikkhus said, and having delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta’s words, they asked the Venerable Sāriputta a further question:

“Could there be, friends, another way in which a noble disciple possesses right view, whose view is upright, who is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma?
“There could be, friend.

When, friend, a noble disciple understands aging-and-death, understands the origin of aging-and-death, understands the cessation of aging-and-death, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death—”
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friend, is aging-and-death? What is the origin of aging-and-death? What is the cessation of aging-and-death? What is the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death?

The aging of each and every being in their respective classes of beings—their decrepitude, brokenness, graying hair, wrinkled skin, the decline of the life-span, and the decay of the faculties—this is aging."
This, friends, is called aging.
And what, friends, is death?

It is the passing away, the perishing, the dissolution, the disappearance, the death, the dying, the completion of time, the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, and the cutting off of the life-faculty of this or that being from this or that class of beings. This is called death.
This, friends, is called death.
Thus, this aging and this death—
this, friends, is called aging-and-death.

With the arising of birth comes the arising of aging and death; with the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of aging and death; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.

When, friend, a noble disciple understands aging and death in this way, and understands the arising of aging and death in this way … [and so on] … he is called a noble disciple who has arrived at the true Dhamma, a noble disciple who has attained the true Dhamma.
He understands thus: "This is the cessation of aging and death"; he understands thus: "This is the way leading to the cessation of aging and death.
Having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust... [and so on] ...he becomes one who makes an end of suffering.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has come to this true Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” he said … [as before] … they asked:
“But could it be, friend … [as before] … ‘It could be, friend.’”

"Friends, when a noble disciple understands birth, understands the origin of birth, understands the cessation of birth, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of birth—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friends, is birth? What is the origin of birth? What is the cessation of birth? What is the practice leading to the cessation of birth?"

Whatever birth, taking birth, descent, coming-to-be, manifestation of the aggregates, and acquisition of the sense-bases there is for this or that being in this or that category of beings—this, friends, is called birth. With the arising of existence comes the arising of birth;
with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth. And it is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path that is the way leading to the cessation of birth, namely: [the rest of the eight factors].
Right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.

Friend, when a noble disciple thus understands birth, thus understands the origin of birth, thus understands the cessation of birth, and thus understands the practice leading to the cessation of birth, he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust.
“Having abandoned [them]... he makes an end of suffering.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” he said... and they questioned him further.
"But could it be, friend... [as before] ...
'It could be, friend.

When, friend, a noble disciple understands existence, understands the origin of existence, understands the cessation of existence, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of existence—'"
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.

But what, friend, is existence? What is the origin of existence? What is the cessation of existence? What is the practice leading to the cessation of existence? There are, friend, these three kinds of existence:"
Existence in the sense-sphere, existence in the fine-material sphere, and existence in the immaterial sphere.

With the arising of clinging comes the arising of existence; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence. The way leading to the cessation of existence is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple understands existence in this way, understands the origin of existence in this way,
understands the cessation of existence in this way, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of existence in this way,
he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust... [and so on] ...and makes an end of suffering.
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
"Excellent, friend," he said... [and] they asked: "But could it be, friend... [and so on].
“It may be so, friend.

But when, friend, a noble disciple understands clinging, understands the origin of clinging, understands the cessation of clinging, and understands the way leading to the cessation of clinging—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.”

"But what, friends, is clinging; what is the origin of clinging; what is the cessation of clinging; and what is the practice leading to the cessation of clinging? There are these four kinds of clinging, friends:
clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self."

With the arising of craving comes the arising of clinging; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of clinging, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple understands clinging in this way, and understands the arising of clinging in this way, ...
In this way he understands the cessation of clinging; in this way he understands the practice leading to the cessation of clinging.
Having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust... [and so on] ...he becomes one who makes an end of suffering.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view, his view is upright, he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, and he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” he said … [as before] … they asked:
“But could it be, friend … [as before] … ‘It could be, friend.’”

"Friends, when a noble disciple understands craving, understands the origin of craving, understands the cessation of craving, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of craving—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friends, is craving? What is the origin of craving? What is the cessation of craving? What is the practice leading to the cessation of craving?"
Friends, there are these six classes of craving:
craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.

With the arising of feeling comes the arising of craving; with the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving. And this very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of craving; that is to say: [the eight factors].
Right view ... right concentration.

When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands craving, thus understands the origin of craving, thus understands the cessation of craving, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of craving, he completely...

“Having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust … [and so on] … he becomes one who makes an end of suffering—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” he said … [and so on] … and they asked him further:
"Could it be, friend... [as before] ...
'It could be, friend.
When, friend, a noble disciple understands feeling, understands the origin of feeling, understands the cessation of feeling, and understands the way leading to the cessation of feeling—"
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friend, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling?
There are these six classes of feeling, friend:"

Feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact. With the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling;
with the cessation of contact there is the cessation of feeling. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands feeling, thus understands the origin of feeling,
thus understands the cessation of feeling, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of feeling,
he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust... [as before] ...and makes an end of suffering.
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
"Excellent, friend," [he said]... and they asked: "But could it be, friend...?"
“It may be so, friend.

But when, friend, a noble disciple understands contact, understands the origin of contact, understands the cessation of contact, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of contact—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
"But what, friends, is contact? What is the origin of contact? What is the cessation of contact? What is the practice leading to the cessation of contact?
Friends, there are these six classes of contact:
eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact."

With the arising of the six sense bases, there is the arising of contact; with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of contact, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple understands contact in this way, and understands the arising of contact in this way, ...
In this way one understands the cessation of contact; in this way one understands the practice leading to the cessation of contact.
Having utterly abandoned the underlying tendency to lust... [and so on] ...he becomes an ender of suffering.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
“Very well, friend,” he replied. … [they] asked: “But could it be, friend, that …?
“… It could be, friend.”

When, friends, a noble disciple understands the six sense bases, understands the origin of the six sense bases, understands the cessation of the six sense bases, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of the six sense bases—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has come to this true Dhamma.

But what, friends, is the sixfold sense base, what is the origin of the sixfold sense base, what is the cessation of the sixfold sense base, and what is the practice leading to the cessation of the sixfold sense base?
These six, friends, are the sense bases:
the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.

With the arising of name-and-form comes the arising of the six sense bases; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of the six sense bases, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple understands the six sense bases in this way, and understands the arising of the six sense bases in this way...
He understands it thus; he understands the cessation of the six sense bases thus; he understands the way leading to the cessation of the six sense bases thus.
Having utterly abandoned the underlying tendency to lust... [as above] ...he becomes one who makes an end of suffering.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
“Excellent, friend,” he said... [as before] ... they asked: “But could it be, friend...?
“It could be, friend.”

"Friend, when a noble disciple understands name-and-form, understands the origin of name-and-form, understands the cessation of name-and-form, and understands the way leading to the cessation of name-and-form—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this true Dhamma. But what, friend, is name-and-form?
What is the origin of name-and-form? What is the cessation of name-and-form? What is the way leading to the cessation of name-and-form?"
Feeling, perception, volition, contact,
and attention— this, friends, is called "name";
and the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements— this is called "form."
This, friends, is called form.
Thus, this which is name and this which is form—
this, friends, is called name-and-form.

With the arising of consciousness comes the arising of name-and-form; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of name-and-form, namely:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple understands name-and-form in this way, and understands the arising of name-and-form in this way, …
In this way he understands the cessation of name-and-form; in this way he understands the practice leading to the cessation of name-and-form.
Having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust... [and so on] ...he becomes one who makes an end of suffering.
To this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has come to this true Dhamma.”
“Excellent, friend,” he said … [as before] … they asked:
“But could it be, friend … [as before] … ‘It could be, friend.’”

"Friends, when a noble disciple understands consciousness, understands the origin of consciousness, understands the cessation of consciousness, and understands the way leading to the cessation of consciousness—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple possesses right view;
his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has come to this true Dhamma. But what, friends, is consciousness?
What is the origin of consciousness? What is the cessation of consciousness? What is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness?"
Friends, there are these six classes of consciousness:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.

With the arising of volitional formations comes the arising of consciousness; with the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness. And this Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, namely: [the eight factors].
Right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.

When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands consciousness, thus understands the origin of consciousness, thus understands the cessation of consciousness, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, he—
“By completely abandoning the underlying tendency to lust...

[and so on] ...he becomes one who makes an end of suffering—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” he said... [and so on] ...and they asked him a question.
"But could it be, friend... [as before] ...
'It could be, friend.

When, friend, a noble disciple understands volitional formations, understands the origin of volitional formations, understands the cessation of volitional formations, and understands the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations—'"
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.

But what, friend, are volitional formations? What is the origin of volitional formations? What is the cessation of volitional formations? What is the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations? There are, friend, these three kinds of volitional formations:"
The bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation.

With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of formations; with the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of formations. The way leading to the cessation of formations is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands volitional formations, thus understands the origin of volitional formations,
thus understands the cessation of volitional formations, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations,
he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, removes the underlying tendency to aversion, and [abandons] the underlying tendency to the view and conceit "I am."

“Having eradicated [the underlying tendencies], having abandoned ignorance, and having generated true knowledge, one makes an end of suffering in this very life—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has arrived at this True Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” they said, and... they asked further:
"Could it be, friend... [as above] ...
'It could be, friend.

When, friend, a noble disciple understands ignorance, understands the origin of ignorance, understands the cessation of ignorance, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of ignorance—'"
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friend, is ignorance? What is the origin of ignorance? What is the cessation of ignorance? What is the practice leading to the cessation of ignorance?

Ignorance, friend, is non-knowing regarding suffering, non-knowing regarding the origin of suffering, non-knowing regarding the cessation of suffering, and non-knowing regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
This, friends, is called ignorance.

With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance; with the cessation of the taints, there is the cessation of ignorance. The way leading to the cessation of ignorance is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands ignorance, thus understands the origin of ignorance, thus understands the cessation of ignorance,
and thus understands the practice leading to the cessation of ignorance,
he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, dispels the underlying tendency to aversion, and uproots the underlying tendency to the conceit and view of "I am."

“By abandoning ignorance and arousing true knowledge, one makes an end of suffering even in this very life—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright, he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, and he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
“Excellent, friend,” those bhikkhus said, rejoicing and expressing their appreciation for the Venerable Sāriputta’s words, and they asked the Venerable Sāriputta a further question:

“Could there be, friend, another way in which a noble disciple possesses right view, whose view is upright, who is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, and who has arrived at this true Dhamma?
“There could be, friend.

When, friend, a noble disciple understands the taints, understands the origin of the taints, understands the cessation of the taints, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of the taints—”
"To this extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
But what, friend, is the taint, what is the origin of the taint, what is the cessation of the taint, and what is the practice leading to the cessation of the taint?
There are these three taints, friend:"
The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.

With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints; with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of the taints. The way leading to the cessation of the taints is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands the taints, thus understands the origin of the taints, thus understands the cessation of the taints,
and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of the taints,
he completely abandons the underlying tendency to lust, dispels the underlying tendency to aversion, and eradicates the underlying tendency to the conceit “I am” and to views.

"By abandoning ignorance and arousing true knowledge, one makes an end of suffering in this very life—to this extent, friend, a noble disciple possesses right view; his view is upright; he is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma; he has come to this true Dhamma.
This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta.
The ninth discourse, “On Right View,” is finished.
